frameworks.name: Reverse Role Model Framework
frameworks.definition: Identify who you don't want to become, extract specific counterexamples from their behaviors, and use those negative way-markers to navigate toward your desired life.

frameworks.name: Directional vs. Absolute Correctness
frameworks.definition: When facing uncertainty and lacking perspective, bias toward taking action in roughly the right direction rather than waiting to identify the perfect path.

frameworks.name: Cheese and Cat Metaphor
frameworks.definition: Life presents rewards (cheese) and threats (cat); when uncertain about the target, move away from pain as a reliable initial direction-setter toward unknown rewards.

claims.text: All human behavior is driven by past reward association; people repeat actions that have rewarded them previously and predict those same actions will deliver reward in the future.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Consistent past reinforcement hardens the behavior prediction and shapes future action selection.

claims.text: Most people attempt to identify the perfect life path or business when they possess zero prior experience, making perspective-based judgment impossible; experience through rapid iteration, not perfectionism, is the only way to build judgment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: for individuals without prior experience in a domain
bounded_by: Does not apply to domains where experimentation is genuinely irreversible or catastrophic (e.g., nuclear engineering, surgery without simulation)

claims.text: When the cat (threat/pain) is unknown and the cheese (target outcome) is undefined, moving in any direction away from the cat increases the likelihood of approaching cheese, even without visibility to the target.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: clear aversion to current state (the cat)
claims.mechanism: Any movement away from a known negative is higher-expectancy than remaining stationary when the positive is invisible.

claims.text: Perfectionism is procrastination masquerading as quality control; the belief that waiting for perfect information before deciding is a decision-making fallacy.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Does not apply to irreversible decisions with genuine catastrophic consequences

claims.text: If someone claims they don't like doing anything, that claim is false; the human brain is neurologically wired to be rewarded for specific behaviors, so every person gravitates toward activities that have rewarded them in the past.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Decreasing action threshold through removal of obstacles (switching from 'cats'—pain mechanisms—to 'cheese'—reward mechanisms) enables people to move toward their desired outcomes more reliably than waiting for motivation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Lowering friction to action and increasing accessibility to rewards compounds action frequency.

claims.text: When starting a business or venture with multiple viable options (e.g., frozen yogurt, test prep, or gym), selecting among them based on personal preference and past competence is sufficient; the specific choice matters less than committing to iterate.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: multiple business options exist with roughly similar market viability
founder has competence in at least one area (e.g., testing, fitness)
bounded_by: Requires sufficient capital or runway to iterate if the first choice doesn't compound

claims.text: Not investing capital is the only guaranteed path to negative real returns, because inflation erodes uninvested cash; therefore, some deployment of capital is economically superior to zero deployment, even under uncertainty.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Inflation compounds as an external forced-cost of capital sitting idle; deployment at any positive expected return beats zero.
bounded_by: Does not apply in severe deflation or in capital-preservation-only contexts (e.g., near end-of-life liquidity needs)

claims.text: Feeling averse to punishment (negative consequences) is a personality trait; using punishment-avoidance as a navigation mechanism (doing only things that reward and avoiding things that don't) is a valid operating philosophy for some people.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: for individuals with high punishment aversion

claims.text: The intersection of personal passion (what rewards you), societal need (what can generate revenue), and personal competence (what you're good at) is the leverage point for building a sustainable business.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

examples.text: Alex Hormozi faced a choice between three business ideas when starting: frozen yogurt (something he enjoyed consuming), test prep (something he was good at from college), and gym ownership (his primary passion). Rather than agonizing over which was 'correct,' he committed to fitness because he liked it, knowing he would at least be doing something he enjoyed. This demonstrates that iteration on a chosen direction matters more than selecting the objectively optimal path when all options have viability.

When Hormozi moved from Baltimore to California, he did not have a specific destination business in mind; he knew he hated his job and hated his city, so he moved geographically away from both (away from the cat). He then committed to fitness because he liked it. The subsequent discovery of his passion for business was not the result of perfect planning but of taking directional action and iterating on reward signals as they emerged.

The Reverse Role Model concept: If no positive exemplars exist in your environment, you can identify people who embody the traits you explicitly don't want (poor relationship dynamics, poor financial management, poor communication patterns) and extract specific 'way-markers' by articulating exactly what you reject. For example: 'I don't want that person's relationship with gambling' becomes a navigation principle toward the opposite behavior.

practices.text: When facing decision paralysis due to lack of perfect information, decrease your action threshold and run rapid iterations to build perspective instead of waiting for certainty.
Identify what punishes or pains you (the cat) and move away from it as your primary navigation mechanism when the target is unclear.
List the people and behaviors you explicitly don't want to become, extract specific counterexamples from them, and use those as way-markers for your own decisions and values.
Structure your daily life to maximize the frequency of activities that reward you and minimize exposure to activities that punish or demotivate you.
